scenes.name: El sonido de Filadelfia
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El imperio de Kenny Gamble y Leon Huff, distribuido por CBS: los O’Jays, los Intruders, Billy Paul y Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes con Teddy Pendergrass, sobre la banda de la casa MFSB (Norman Harris, Bobby Eli, Ronnie Baker, Earl Young), la más exitosa de los setenta; su «TSOP» fue la sintonía de Soul Train. Los O’Jays fueron el altavoz del comentario social de Gamble: «Back Stabbers» (1972), Ship Ahoy (1974) con su travesía en un barco negrero, «For the Love of Money» (que el éxito convirtió en música de centro comercial), Survival, Family Reunion. Después de 1976 desapareció el mensaje del soul, y con Gloria Gaynor y Donna Summer la frontera entre el disco, el funk y el soul se borró.

podcast.title: Payola Scandal (1975)
podcast.body: While Kenny Gamble faced a payola scandal in 1975 and incurred a fine, Leon Huff was not penalized during the investigation. "In the end Gamble had a slap on the wrist fine assessed and huff didn't."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Architects of Disco
podcast.body: Despite their later disavowal of disco, Gamble and Huff are recognized as two of its primary architects, notably through their innovative production work on songs like "The Love I Lost," which introduced the seminal "four-on-the-floor" beat. "Gamble and Huff rejected Disco later in the decade, but that does not change the fact that they were two of its architects."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Enduring Philosophy on Message Music
podcast.body: Even 50 years after their initial success, Huff and Gamble remain committed to their core philosophy that the message embedded in music is paramount, striving to create not only musically appealing tracks but also songs that inspire and enlighten their listeners. "They wanted to make something more than music that sounded good."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: John Lennon of 1970s
podcast.body: Leon Huff, in partnership with Kenny Gamble, was characterized as the John Lennon of the 1970s, signifying his crucial role as a prolific and impactful songwriter and producer within the Philadelphia soul genre. "Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff were the Paul McCartney and John Lennon of the 1970s."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Motown Study Trip
podcast.body: Leon Huff accompanied Kenny Gamble on Gamble's first ever airplane journey, a trip to Detroit specifically intended to tour the Motown facilities, which served as a crucial model for their aspirations to establish their own record label. "Gamble's first plane ride ever was with Huff on a trip to Detroit to tour Motown."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: PIR Founding
podcast.body: Huff, together with Kenny Gamble, was offered a deal by CBS Records president Clive Davis, leading to the creation of Philadelphia International Records, an initiative motivated by Davis's aim for CBS to become a dominant force in the "Black Music Market." "Clive Davis, the president of CBS Records, offered Gamble and Huff a deal that allows them to create Philadelphia international records."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Songwriting Partnership with Kenny Gamble
podcast.body: Following a chance encounter in Philadelphia's Schubert building, Huff and Gamble rapidly formed a successful songwriting team, with Huff composing the music at the piano while Gamble penned the lyrics, despite neither possessing the ability to read musical notation. "Gamble wrote the lyrics, Huff wrote the music, sitting at the piano, even though neither could read music."
